# Open findings register

Things measured, recorded, and **not fixed** — with no line item in any stage
of [NSOT_PLAN.md](NSOT_PLAN.md).

**Why this file exists.** Each of these was written into `CLAUDE.md` or a
stage document at the moment it was found, in prose, beside the thing it was
found next to. That is the right place to explain *why* something is true and
the wrong place to keep a list: prose accumulates invisibly, and the only way
to know what is outstanding was to have been present when each one was
recorded. The register is the list; the prose stays where it is and is linked.

**Rules.** An item leaves this file by being fixed, by being scheduled into a
stage, or by being closed with a reason. **A row that is fixed moves to
Closed in the same turn** (2026-09-28: 31 of 92 rows in the open sections
were done and had never moved, so the open count read about twice the work;
`tests/test_register_hygiene.py` now refuses a done row in an open
section). **A live exposure is listed here even when a stage owns it**: a
row with a home stopped counting as a finding, and NSOT_PLAN 6.1 sat outside
the triage built to catch it (C143). It does not leave by being
forgotten.

**The open count is a claim about DEFERRED work** (the operator, 2026-09-28). A row a stage owns lives in *Scheduled out of the register*, naming the stage, and leaves the open count; the stage's plan lists it. The open sections hold only what waits: A, B, UNKNOWN, and C deferred to Stage 9. Twice the register misled us about its own size (31 done rows never moved; then 26 of 61 open rows that were stage work), and both times the fix was a rule a test enforces: `test_register_hygiene.py` refuses an open row whose bucket places it in a stage other than Stage 9.

**The stopping rule for a sweep** (the operator, 2026-09-28, applied by default). A sweep may REGISTER whatever it finds, and only A items it finds are fixed in the same pass. Everything else waits, however cheap and however near the code being edited. A items found by fixing A items had begun to feed themselves (C155, C157, C158, C160), and "we are already in the file" is how a fix grows a second fix nobody triaged. C161 is the rule's first application: found inside C160's fix, in the same function, and left. Anything recorded as *"not applied"*, *"noted, not yet
addressed"*, *"recorded as a gap"* or *"left open"* belongs here on the same
day it is written.

**A register is only current if the reader checks the head.** A stale read
of a maintained file cannot be told apart from a stale file. On 2026-09-25 this
register was read at `1b9b4d3` while the repository was four commits ahead,
and three items already closed were raised again as open. That is the failure
this file exists to prevent, arriving through the reader rather than the
document. Before acting on an item, run `git log -1 -- docs/OPEN_FINDINGS.md`
and compare it with the head you are reading.

Status: **open** unless stated. Last reviewed 2026-10-07 (the charter triage below).

## Triage, 2026-09-28: every open row placed

**The rule (the operator's): a finding's SEVERITY is a claim about the world,
and claims about the world are measured, not assumed.** The findings that
turned out to be live exposure all read as tidying until something was
measured: C95 (masking, and it was a secret in a shared system), C141 (a code
default, and it was a published value) and C136 (cosmetic, and the import
could not be performed for 9 hours). The inverse held too (C135, C138, C142
real and harmless). So the classification depends on facts, and a row whose
severity rests on an unmeasured one is UNKNOWN until it is measured.

**The buckets, each a stated criterion:**
- **A, LIVE EXPOSURE**: true in the world now, and time makes it worse: a
  secret readable, a device unmanageable, data being lost.
- **B, BLOCKING**: something specific cannot be built or run until it is
  fixed. The row names what. If nothing is blocked, it is not B.
- **UNKNOWN**: could be A, and the fact that decides it has not been
  measured. Named with the one measurement and its cost.
- **C, EVERYTHING ELSE**: real, correctly recorded, and the tool works
  without it.

**Before sorting:** 92 rows sat in the open sections. **31 were already done**
and moved to Closed: 29 on their own row's evidence (FIXED, DONE or closed in
the status cell, never moved), and 2 measured done on the host tonight (C17's
URLs are set; E4's drift checker is enabled and ran at 05:47Z). C141 was
merged into C39, and C143 was added. **61 open.**

**The operator's question: was the triage a one-time sort, or do new rows
default to C? It was a one-time sort.** The re-triage's split (functional,
lab, minor) answers WHERE work goes, and it silently replaced the severity
axis (A, B, UNKNOWN, C) for every row recorded after it: C144, C145, C147 and
C148 each got a home and no bucket. By the criterion, **C148 is B (it blocks
the onboard-to-deploy loop, the product's central one)**, and **C147 was A
when it was recorded** (latent: the next device arriving with an RW community
would have had it written into the first permanent record; fixed the same
turn).

**Now structural:** every row in a live section, "Scheduled" included, opens
its status cell with ONE bucket, `**[A|B|UNKNOWN|C …; sorted <date>]**`. B
names what it blocks and whether that is on the critical path; UNKNOWN names
the measurement that would settle it; C names its kind (F functional, L
deferred for the lab, M minor) and its home.
`tests/test_register_hygiene.py` refuses a row without one, with a control.
**A new finding gets its bucket the turn it is recorded, with the criterion
applied, never assumed.**

| B9 | **CONFIRMED 2026-09-26: the off-box B2 key can destroy the backups it writes, without `deleteFiles`.** Run by the operator: `rclone delete -vv --include b2probe.txt` printed `Deleted` with no refusal, the normal listing was empty, and `--b2-versions` held the hidden version. `writeFiles` allows a HIDE, and the lifecycle deletes hidden versions a day later, so a compromised NMAS erases every off-box copy within 24 h. The first test (a single-file path: exit 0, file still listed) passed while proving nothing, because rclone's single-file check needs `readFiles`, so the file was never touched. **Fix: B2 Object Lock, Governance mode, default retention 16 days: the lifecycle's hide-after (15) plus its hide-to-delete (1)**, so no hide can delete anything sooner than the lifecycle would have. (First recorded as 15, which was a day short; corrected 2026-09-26) (docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §4). The semantics are from B2's documentation as understood here, and a five-step probe plan measures them before real data depends on them. **Closes when** step 4 of that plan shows a hidden LOCKED version surviving the lifecycle, and step 5 shows a governance bypass works. | **[C, L (Object Lock enabled, by the operator's account; not re-measured here); sorted 2026-09-28]** operator's step (measure, then enable) | docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §4 |
| B10 | **Nothing checks that the bucket's lock retention covers its lifecycle window.** **Decided 2026-09-26 (operator): a read-only key**, scoped to the bucket, which is ALSO the retrieval key (docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §6): one key, on the laptop to fetch and on the NMAS to check. It may live on the NMAS because everything it can read, the NMAS already holds unencrypted. It cannot write, so it cannot undermine what it checks, and a compromised NMAS can use it only to look. A manual check in the B2 UI was rejected: it is done once and never again, and this pair is exactly what drifts when one is changed and the other forgotten. **The property to check is not "both are 15"** but **lock retention >= daysFromUploadingToHiding + daysFromHidingToDeleting**. Shorter fails, because files become deletable before the lifecycle removes them: the hole re-opening silently. Longer warns, because the lock has silently become the retention. The design: (1) expected effects derived from the program (an interface it shuts going down and the adjacencies over it dropping; one it brings up, and new adjacencies on it), shown in the plan; (2) declared effects for what cannot be inferred (a moved adjacency, a decommissioned session), with a reason, in the confirmed plan and the record; (3) verify the intended end state within a settle window (a declared move whose adjacency never re-forms is the failure); (4) unexpected effects still fail (an untouched interface down, an adjacency on an untouched interface lost, the device unreachable); (5) roll back promptly, after a short measured settle, only on an UNEXPECTED hard failure; with nothing hard failed the hold-time wait stays. | **[C, functional; sorted 2026-10-05]** **BOARD APPROVED 2026-10-06 (the operator, canvas v54), with these choices:** (1) THREE declarations: an adjacency moves; a session ends (decommission); routes are expected to change (no "new neighbour" option for now); (2) the settle before an unexpected hard failure rolls back is ONE installation-wide default that networks inherit (P.8's model), overridden only where a network must, MEASURED per platform from the devices' own flap-to-recovery history (syslog, SNMP) rather than guessed, 10 s in this lab until measured, and the result names the settle it used; (3) an undeclared neighbour forming is a NOTE when additional and a FAILURE when it replaces a declared expectation (naming both). The agent's part is Stage 8's (NSOT_PLAN 8.13). Built after C512, the GUI batch and C500. **Phase 1 BUILT 2026-10-06:** interfaces judged by name against the program's derived effects (`expected_effects`), first; an untouched interface lost gets the `unexpected` settle (10 s, `verify_settle_windows`, the installation default) and then fails at once, the neighbour windows, BGP's hold time and the route window skipped; an interface the program brings up must be up; counting only when a read names none. **Phase 2 BUILT 2026-10-06** (reordered: the plan's derived effects come before verify honours them, since a derived adjacency effect is not visible in the program; **the swap APPROVED by the operator, 2026-10-06: accepting adjacency drops silently would have repeated Part 5.3 unseen**): `expected_effects.for_device` derives, from the program and committed intent, each adjacency on an interface the program shuts (OSPF and OSPFv3 by interface) and each BGP session sourced from one or to a peer on its subnet, and an OSPF adjacency that may form on one it brings up; the device deploy card draws them under Expected effects; verify leaves exactly those out of each protocol's comparison by identity (router-id, BGP address) and the hold watch's baseline; an interface the program shuts must be down. **Phase 3 BUILT 2026-10-06:** the three declarations on the device deploy card (an adjacency moves: one the program drops, to an interface it brings up with OSPF on it; a session ends: an adjacency intent gives outside what the program drops; routes are expected to change), each with a reason of the authorisations' shape, carried between plans, checked against what the plan offers (`expected_effects.offers`, `declared_from`), folded into the confirm's hash, checked again at apply (refused by name when they no longer fit) and in `_deploy_one`, and recorded in the receipt; verify requires a declared move to re-form on its interface within the protocol's settle window (OSPF's rows now keep their interface), failing when it re-forms elsewhere or someone new forms there instead, naming both; an ended session is an expected drop; a declared route change is a note, not a failure; an undeclared additional adjacency is a note; the result card draws each move's outcome and the notes. The v1 JSON plan and apply take no declarations (the v1 rule). **Phase 4, 2026-10-06:** BUILT: the deploy card's "What verify checks" table (`expected_effects.verify_checks`: each check names its object, what it expects and when it reads, from the plan's derived and declared effects, the network's settle windows, the verify scope, BGP's hold time per neighbour in the captured config, and the pipeline's own route floor); the receipt records how verify compared the interfaces (by name or counted), the expected effects, the settle an unexpected loss got and whether verify failed at once, and the result card says them in words. NOT BUILT: the batch preview's Expected effects (no board draws it: drawn first, with C537's mockup). MEASURED, and not enough: the per-platform settle from the devices' own history: Loki's 14 days hold 22 interface state changes, 3 of them shutdowns, and ONE bounce (r3, down 14 s, longer than the 10 s settle); one sample of one platform decides nothing, so the measurement is made on purpose on the throwaway (THROWAWAY_SESSION.md Part 4c), and the 10 s stays the inherited default until then. | C695 | **r4 drops traffic for r3's ISP peering address while advertising a default into OSPF** (found 2026-10-12 by C693's measurement, through Mercury's reads engine; the register searched first). r1, r2 and s4 split traffic for 198.51.100.1 over their OSPF default's two next hops, r3 and r4; r4's own `show ip cef 198.51.100.1` is "0.0.0.0/0 no route", and r3's for 198.51.100.3 (r4's peering) the same: each edge router originates a default "always" without holding one, and neither carries the other's peering /31. So a flow hashed to the wrong edge router for the other's peering address is dropped. Judged LAB against the charter: the lab network's routing design, not Mercury's; the trace reports it correctly. **Measured 2026-10-12 03:22 to 03:27 UTC (the operator's list), read-only through Mercury's reads engine on r3 and r4 only, each read recorded:** (1) **neither edge holds a real default**: `show ip route 0.0.0.0` is "% Network not in table" on both, and both carry `default-information originate always` under `router ospf 1` and `ipv6 router ospf 1` (OSPFv3 also `redistribute static`). (2) **r5 advertises three prefixes to each edge**, the same to both: 8.8.8.8/32, 10.255.1.15/32 (r5's loopback) and 203.0.113.0/31; each edge holds all three from its own eBGP session (no iBGP between r3 and r4; nothing redistributed between BGP and OSPF). Each edge advertises 0 IPv4 prefixes to r5 (`prefix-list NO-PRIVATE out`, no `network` under IPv4). (3) **Nothing r5 advertises is blackholed**: Path… from r1 and r2 to 8.8.8.8, 203.0.113.1 and 10.255.1.15 splits over r3 and r4, and both hand it to r5; r1 pings 8.8.8.8 5/5 from its loopback and from Gi2, and r3 and r4 each 5/5 (so r5 routes the fleet's addresses back by means Mercury cannot read). (4) **Only the two peering /31s are affected**: r1 pings 198.51.100.1 0/5 (its flow hashes to r4) and 198.51.100.3 5/5. An address r5 does not advertise (192.0.2.1) is dropped at whichever edge: there is no real default anywhere, while the fleet's OSPF says there is. **The fix options, each the operator's pick (no device change made):** (a) **the peering /31s into OSPF, passive** (`network 198.51.100.0 0.0.0.1 area 0` and `passive-interface GigabitEthernet2` on r3; `198.51.100.2 0.0.0.1` on r4; the OSPFv3 equivalent for the IPv6 peerings): every router learns each /31 at the edge that holds it, so that address goes only there; no adjacency with r5; fixes exactly this symptom and changes nothing else. (b) **a conditional default** (`default-information originate always route-map <map>`, the map matching a prefix learned from r5): an edge whose eBGP session is down stops attracting traffic; failover, not the /31s. (c) **iBGP r3–r4 with next-hop-self** (update-source Loopback0, over OSPF): each edge also learns r5's routes through the other, so a flow sent to an edge whose own session is down still leaves; the /31s only if each edge also advertises its connected /31 into BGP (`network 198.51.100.0 mask 255.255.255.254`). (a) is the smallest that fixes C695; (b) or (c) adds failover. Each is a deploy through Mercury (intent, preview, verify), the BGP or OSPF settle windows applying. | **[C, lab design; sorted 2026-10-12]** measured; the fix is the operator's pick of (a), (b), (c) or a combination. | the lab's r3 and r4 configuration |

None of them holds a list: a device dict carries none. Step 4a reads them as the Default network's, by name (`list_settings.default_layer`, in `tests/test_network_settings_read_for_a_list.py`'s inventory). The paths that do hold a list read their own: the pipeline's failure capture and rollback read-back, a rotation's capture, the deploy's unchanged-measure. **Bucket C:** one list exists, so nothing is wrong today. With a second list, its device sessions would wait Default's bound; a slower network would read as an unreadable one, and a faster one would wait longer than set. **The fix:** a device dict carries its list from `load_saved_devices(list)`, and the SSH layer reads the device's own network; each Default-layer read leaves the inventory as it goes | **[C, functional → P.8; sorted 2026-10-05]** P.8, with step 5 (readers loop lists) | NSOT_P8_DESIGN.md, section 6, step 4 |

| C189 | **The app log records an ERROR, "The WebSocket transport is not available", that began today** (found reading the host log for C188, 2026-09-28). engine.io logs it when a client asks to upgrade to a WebSocket and the server's async mode cannot serve one, so the client stays on long-polling. The live-data contract still works over that transport. Counted per log file on the host: 0 in the files starting 05:17 and 08:49, 4 in the one from 14:24, and 6 since 22:03. So something that shipped today makes the browser try to upgrade. An ERROR for expected behaviour teaches the reader of the log to skip ERRORs (C26's shape). **The cause, measured 2026-09-30 (via LAN, read-only): the host has no `simple-websocket`.** Under Flask-SocketIO's `threading` async mode (app.py:141) the server can serve a WebSocket only with that package installed; the laptop has it (1.1.0), the host's lock (`requirements.lock`, generated on the host) does not, so every upgrade the browser asks for fails and the channel stays on long-polling. The contract still holds over long-polling, as recorded. The fix is the serving stack: the production server keeps the threading mode, `simple-websocket` joins the lock, and nginx proxies the upgrade. **Measured again 2026-10-03 (via LAN, read-only, the app log since 05:31Z), after the operator saw `data-live="unknown"` in the served page and 14,010 `/socket.io/` requests with one 101:** 105 handshakes, all 200; 105 distinct sessions; 4,975 long-polling exchanges on them, all 200; no WebSocket request in the app's log. The channel connects over long-polling, so the browser's `connect` fires. The served page's `unknown` is the value before any script runs (`base.html`); the script redraws it every second from the socket's state, so only the live DOM can say connected (`document.getElementById('nmas-live').dataset.live`). Its served word was "Live" (C390, fixed). | **[C, functional → Stage 9; sorted 2026-09-30]** 2026-09-28 | Stage 9's 9.S, the production serving stack (NSOT_PLAN.md) |

The two switches with the slowest measured clocks (C9) miss most: s3 (0.55 to 0.61) 1,540 and s4 (0.75) 227, against 161 to 192 for every other device (r5, retired partway, 91). That is a correlation (a starved vIOS answers slowly), not a proven cause. **A threshold measured from those runs:** at two consecutive misses the fleet's offline runs fall from 2,946 to 195, and at three to 99; the log's whole-second times make that approximate, and a reader counting misses makes it exact. Genuine outages look different: runs over 60 s mostly come 6 to 8 devices at once (2026-09-26 00:12, 08:33 and 08:41; 2026-09-27 08:42), which is the path to the fleet rather than a device. For about thirty seconds the operator believed the restore had cut in-band management. r2 was fine: ping 5 of 5, 23 to 31 ms. So the problem is not that the dot is noisy. So the dot's claim is "the device's SSH listener accepted a connection within 2 s", made under the name "ping", with the failure of the ICMP half invisible. | C106 | **CLIs that stop half-way, leaving a state nobody is told about** (the operator's question after `nmas-deploy` moved the checkout and could not restart, 2026-09-27; surveyed by reading every script, 1a VERIFIED and FIXED, the rest from the code read and not yet verified). (1a) `rotate()` set "rotated and committed" whatever `_commit` answered and then DELETED the staging copy, so a failed credential-store write left a device holding a password recorded nowhere, reported as "live and recorded": fixed (state `ROTATED_NOT_RECORDED`, the copy kept and named, danger first, a job-health row). Recovery is by hand from the kept copy: a `--record-staged` path does not exist yet. (1b) the persist chain's `oxidized_row` ran `sudo -n` with no pre-check (the operator, next after C70: an unchecked sudo in the rotation path is B15's shape). Verified: a refused `sudo -n` printed nothing on stdout, the stage parsed `{}`, and the chain failed with NO reason after the device was already rotated and committed. **FIXED 2026-09-27**: preflight asks `sudo -n -l <helper>` before anything changes the device and refuses naming the exact sudoers line; the stage checks sudo's exit code and names a refusal; an answer without `ok` is not success. Measured on the host: the narrow rule exists and the service runs as the user it covers, so nothing is refused there today. (The danger sentence printing last remains.) (2) `oxidized-to-config.sh` can overwrite some labs' startup configs and then fail a later copy, the read-back or the commit; a failed backup is ignored (`cp -r … 2>/dev/null`), and a failed commit still ends "Startup-configs updated". (3) `nmas-retire` clears the credential before a step that can fail, and its refusal omits what was already done (it is resumable). (4) `nmas-netbox-backup` pruned old backups before the new one had shipped, and by AGE alone: while shipping failed, the local copies were the only copies and were deleted as they aged, so a failed run left fewer backups than before (the operator: fix first). **FIXED 2026-09-27**: ship first, prune last, and an expired backup is deleted only once recorded as shipped to every destination its tier needs (`shipped.json`); an unshipped one is kept, named in the run and first in `--status`, and retried each run. **Deletion is keyed on the PROPERTY, not a proxy for it** (the operator): age was the proxy, existence elsewhere is the property, the register's recurring lesson applied to retention. And the retry converts a permanent gap into a delay: a missed daily used to be lost for good and now ships late, so the off-box copy's completeness no longer depends on nothing having failed on any given night. (5) `nmas-bulk-intent` and three `nsot_*` repair scripts leave written, uncommitted files, reported as "REFUSED", which reads as nothing having happened (the standing rule inverted: the message says nothing happened, the filesystem disagrees, and the person acts on the message). **Bulk intent FIXED 2026-09-27**: a failed commit puts every written file back as committed and says "nothing changed", or leads with LEFT UNCOMMITTED naming the paths; the three repair scripts remain. Also: `nmas-deploy` exits with a traceback and no audit row if `git fetch` or `merge` fails; `nmas-persist-native` exits 1 ("not persisted") if recording raises after the device saved. **The pattern (the operator's):** a tool that does part of an operation and stops, and tells the person running it but not the exit code or anything that watches. `nmas-deploy` is fixed (it refuses before moving when it cannot restart, exit 6; a failed restart leads with MIXED VERSION; a `running-version` job-health row). **The ordering, checked against each remaining item** (the operator's question after 1b, 2026-09-27: does the irreversible part come first, with the blocker found second?). Read from the code: **(2) the containerlab sync: YES, three times.** A lab's startup configs are overwritten, and a LATER lab's copy failure is found afterwards. The loop continues and the count check refuses with exit 1, while the first lab stays overwritten and uncommitted. The next run's reconcile can record it late. The per-lab backup runs as `cp -r … 2>/dev/null; rsync …`. The `;` means a failed backup does not stop the overwrite it exists to protect. Whether a destination can commit (repo present, git identity) is found only after every file is written. The run then ends with "Startup-configs updated." as its LAST line, after the failure block. The fix has three parts. Check every destination's preconditions before copying any. Gate each rsync on its backup (`&&`). Lead with the state. **(3) nmas-retire: YES.** It clears the device's credential override FIRST (irreversible: the value is gone), then writes the declaration, then commits. The commit can fail (`manifest.release`, git), and on failure the device is still in the inventory, managed, with its override gone. The CLI then leads with "REFUSED:", which reads as nothing having happened. The fix is to commit first (the commit already puts the tree back on failure), delete both credentials last, and have a stop lead with what was done. **(5) the three repair scripts: NO, the same symptom by a different mechanism.** Nothing irreversible happens before the commit. They write working-tree files, and a failed commit leaves them written. The fix is bulk intent's: put the files back as committed. **`nmas-persist-native`: NO.** The device save is the operation, and a failed record after it is a false REPORT ("not persisted"), not a late-found blocker. **`nmas-deploy`'s fetch/merge: NO.** A failed `merge --ff-only` leaves the checkout unmoved, so only the traceback is wrong. **1b's danger sentence printing last** is the report half of the same shape, and stays open. **(2) the containerlab sync, FIXED 2026-09-27 (the operator's order: the `;` first):** a lab is copied only after its OWN backup succeeded (the `;` let a failed backup go on to overwrite the configs it protected). A failure is named for its step: file list, BACKUP FAILED, or COPY FAILED after the backup (restore from it). Attempts are counted apart from successes, so a failed lab is no longer blamed on the loop ("ran fewer times") or the copy ("reported success ... do not match"), both false. Only the copied labs are read back and committed. The staged files are kept while any lab failed, and the summary leads with "NOT ALL LABS UPDATED: N of M" and exits 3. Tested by executing the shipped region under bash against real directories, with one lab's backup refused; a control that stops the failed backup from stopping its copy fails both tests. **The second half, FIXED the same day (the operator: fix it with the rest; the third script with this shape):** before any copy, each destination is asked whether it can take a commit (its git directory writable, no `index.lock` left behind; the identity rides on every commit already). A lab that cannot is refused BEFORE its copy, named "CANNOT COMMIT (reason); NOTHING was copied". A lab with no repository is still copied and reported NOT VERSIONED, a declared state named every run. Tested with a repository holding a stale `index.lock`; control: the skip removed fails it. | **[C, F → 7.3 for (3): retire clears the credential before a commit that can fail, so a failed retire leaves a device MANAGED WITH NO CREDENTIAL (A if it fires); 7.3 builds retire as an operation, commit first, and (3) is its acceptance. The alert rules use the same query, so a broken applet's own error read as a sign of life: the unsafe direction. Now anchored on the line's exact form, `%HA_EM-\d-LOG: NMAS-HEARTBEAT: NMAS-HEARTBEAT`. Over 6 h of the whole fleet those were the only two shapes naming the applet. **Also:** every gap spanning the device's own `%SYS-5-CONFIG_I` is excluded, because re-entering the applet restarts its timer and leaves a gap between one and two intervals: under the long-gap cut, and enough to make any maintenance window leave INSEPARABLE behind it. Re-measured live: all nine devices `measured`, s4 at window 1005 s. **The generated rules file was an untracked file in the live checkout** (the script's default output path), so committing it would have aborted the next pull. It is now gitignored, and `--check`'s help no longer calls it "committed". **Operator step:** regenerate and reinstall the rules; the installed ones still carry the substring query. |
| C20 | A settings-route test failed intermittently, echoing `kea_username` as `''`. | 2026-09-25 | **Two causes, both measured and fixed, neither the one first suspected.** **(1) The test failure: import-time binding.** `modules.integrations.base` binds `get_setting` by name. When `test_onboard_plan.py` ran before anything imported `app`, `base` was first imported inside that file's `lab` fixture, while `settings_schema.get_setting` was a lambda answering unlisted keys with the schema default. `base` kept the lambda. An import hook recorded the import, on the main thread, with the lambda bound. The order was deterministic: 3 of 3 failed with that file first, 2 of 2 passed with it second. The **streaks were my subset command**: `grep` in the tool shell is a parallel `ugrep` and returns files in varying order. `conftest.py` now imports `app` before any test runs, as the program does, and a subprocess test runs the failing order. **(2) Found while chasing it, and worse: concurrent settings writes CORRUPTED the file.** A probe recorded every write during a failing run and saw only the route's own two, both correct, so the redaction refresh and the background threads were ruled out by measurement. But `save_user_settings` used one temp name for every writer, and no read-modify-write held a lock. Two threads × 150 writes left `user_settings.json` unreadable in 2 of 2 runs, and the unreadable-file guard then refused every write. Fixed: a per-write `mkstemp`, and `config.settings_lock()` (an RLock, plus `flock` across processes) around all four read-modify-write sites. After the fix: 300 of 300 keys, threads and processes, 3 of 3 runs. An AST scan requires the lock in any function that both loads and saves. The general-settings POST was one of the four, and it **bypasses `write_settings()`**, so CLAUDE.md's *one write path* was not true. |
| B4 | NetBox's env files were world-readable (0664). | 2026-09-25 | **Closed on evidence.** The operator ran `chmod 600`; measured later that evening, all four `env/*.env` read `600` and `netbox-docker-netbox-1` was `Up 6 hours (healthy)`. NetBox also answered the heartbeat generator's queries after the change. The backup writes its copies `0600` regardless (pinned). |
| C18 | Commits from a CLI never pushed. | 2026-09-25 | **Fixed.** Post-commit hooks run on daemon threads, and a short-lived process (`nmas-retire`) exited under its own push: r5's retire commit `3592113` never reached `<repo>`, and nothing recorded a failure. Hook runners are now joined at exit, bounded at 90 s; an unfinished one is named on stderr as "the commit is local and may not have been pushed". Proven in a real subprocess, with a control. `3592113` pushes with the next commit from the app, or by hand. |
| C19 | Secret stores the checker could not see, and their modes. | 2026-09-25 | **Fixed in code.** `nmas-check-secret-storage` classifies EVERY file under `data/` (secret: must be 0600 / no-secret: scanned / config-bearing / plain), and an undeclared file fails the run, so a new store is noticed on its first run. Outside `data/` it checks a declared list (rclone.conf, the NetBox env files, the backup push key). Live: 773 files classified, 0 unclassified, and **5 loose secret stores found**: `credential_profiles.json`, `devices.csv` plus two old copies, and `secret.key` (Flask's session key), all 0664, beneath a run that had printed "every file holding a secret is owner-only". The credential store's and devices.csv's writers and `secret.key`'s creation now go through `open_secure`, so the next write heals them. The two old CSV copies and `secret.key` are never rewritten, so they need `chmod 600` by hand. Actual exposure was limited: `data/` is 0700. |
| C16 | The per-platform heartbeat window was the wrong shape. | 2026-09-25 | **Built: per-device windows** (`scripts/nmas-heartbeat-rules`). Each device's window is the midpoint of its own separable band, measured from its Loki arrivals, with misses in the history excluded. A new device gets a **provisional** window, labelled as such in the rule itself and derived from the fleet's slowest measured rate; a device with an empty band is named `inseparable`. `--check` re-measures hourly on its own timer, declared in `job_health`, and names `STALE RATE`, `PROVISIONAL READY`, `UNMEASURABLE`, `MISSING` and `EXTRA`. **Live: nine measured windows**, r1–r4 and r6 750 s, s1 797, s2 799, s3 1286, s4 996; r5 named not expected; `--check` current for all nine. Controls shown failing. |
| C15 | A write whose commit failed was stranded, and the run that stranded it reported success. | 2026-09-25 | **Fixed in `scripts/oxidized-to-config.sh`.** Every run reconciles every managed file BEFORE the early exit and before any copy. A dirty file is committed ("recorded late") only when it is byte-identical to `render_device`'s output for the Oxidized version its own header names; anything else is REFUSED for that device, neither committed nor overwritten, named, and the run exits 3 (including on the "nothing to copy" path). The per-lab commit now adds and commits only the job's own files by path. The executed tests found their own fixture could not exhibit the version case (its second poll changed only a stripped comment); fixed, and the control then fired. r6's stranded file was committed by hand by the operator. |
| C11 | Deleting a device left it half-managed in five places; there was no retire. | 2026-09-25 | **Built: `scripts/nmas-retire` / `modules/nsot/retire.py`.** Clear the override, declare the startup file deliberately unmapped, then one commit that removes intent and golden and releases the identity (history kept), then the CSV row LAST, and only against a break-glass record holding the device's CURRENT credential (a refusal, not a step). It states every time what it will NOT do: NetBox kept, Oxidized polling, startup frozen, device config unchanged, backups kept, the pooled session. It is resumable, and a failed commit puts the tree back. **ACCEPTANCE PASSED 2026-09-25 on the real device (operator):** commit `3592113`; zero r5 in host_vars, golden, devices.csv and the manifest; the approval withdrawn naming its cause ("device 'r5' is no longer bound"); `cisco_iosxe/base.j2` binds r1, r2, r3, r4, r6; credential overrides: 1 (r6's), 0 unclaimed. Declared-unmapped on its first real use: `produced : 9`, `declared : 1 — r5: ISP device outside our administrative boundary… (<user>, 2026-09-25T20:33:27Z)`. Found beside it and fixed: `nmas-clab-targets --device` unpacked 3 columns from 6-column rows and crashed on the first. |
